# Myasthenia gravis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Cardiothoracic surgery > Myasthenia gravis*

[Original Article Link](/library/DR016f)

---

## Summary

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disease of the <u>neuromuscular junction</u> (NMJ) characterized by <u>muscle weakness</u> that worsens with activity and improves with rest. MG is caused by <u>autoantibodies</u> directed against postsynaptic molecules, most commonly <u>acetylcholine receptors</u> (AchR), resulting in impaired neuromuscular transmission. Women are more frequently affected; ∼ 10–15% of cases are associated with <u>thymoma</u>. The most common initial symptom is ocular <u>muscle weakness</u> (e.g., <u>ptosis</u> and/or <u>diplopia</u>), with progression to generalized <u>weakness</u> typically occurring within two years. The diagnosis is clinical and confirmed by <u>antibody</u> testing and electromyographic evaluation. Treatment of choice consists of <u>acetylcholinesterase inhibitors</u>; <u>immunosuppressive drugs</u> can be added if symptoms persist. All patients with MG should be screened for <u>thymoma</u> with CT chest. Thymectomy is indicated for patients with confirmed <u>thymoma</u>. Acute exacerbations, as seen in myasthenic crises, are generally treated with either IV <u>immunoglobulins</u> or plasma exchange.

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u>: most common <u>neuromuscular junction</u> disorder [[1]](/library/ZObZIF)

* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (3:2)

* Peak <u>incidence</u> [[2]](/library/AUXRfx)

* <u>♂</u> : 40–70 years

* <u>♀</u> : 20–40 years




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

### Autoimmune




* <u>Autoantibodies</u> directed against postsynaptic <u>acetylcholine receptors</u> or <u>receptor</u>-associated <u>proteins</u>  

* Most common: <u>acetylcholine receptor antibodies</u> (<u>AChR-Ab</u>)

* Less common: <u>muscle-specific tyrosine kinase antibodies</u> (<u>MuSK-Ab</u>), <u>lipoprotein</u> <u>receptor</u>-related protein <u>antibodies</u> (LRP4-Ab), or no detectable <u>antibodies</u>

* Association with other autoimmune diseases, including:

* <u>Hashimoto thyroiditis</u>

* <u>Rheumatoid arthritis</u>

* <u>Sarcoidosis</u>

* <u>Systemic lupus erythematosus</u>





> [!TIP]
> A minority of patients with myasthenia gravis have no detectable <u>antibodies</u> (i.e., seronegative MG). 100% of patients with <u>thymoma</u> have <u>autoantibodies</u>.




### Associated conditions [[3]](/library/SfXylx)




* <u>Thymoma</u> (the most common primary <u>tumor</u> in the <u>anterior mediastinum</u>) in 10–15% of patients

* <u>Thymic</u> <u>hyperplasia</u> in 65% of patients

* <u>Graft-versus-host reaction</u> after <u>allogeneic stem cell transplantation</u> (especially in children)

---

## Classification

* Ocular myasthenia: only the extraocular and/or <u>eyelid</u> muscles

* Generalized myasthenia

* All <u>skeletal muscles</u> may be involved.

* Especially ocular, bulbar, limb, and respiratory muscles

---

## Pathophysiology

### <u>Thymus</u> involvement



* Muscle-like (myoid) cells in the <u>thymus</u> express <u>AChR</u> → autoreactive targeting by <u>T cells</u> → production of <u>acetylcholine receptor antibodies</u> (<u>AChR antibodies</u>)




### Acetylcholine receptor antibodies [[4]](/library/ffXklx)




* Responsible for inhibition of <u>signal transduction</u> at the <u>neuromuscular junction</u> (NMJ)

* <u>Antibodies</u> target postsynaptic <u>AChRs</u> of normal muscle cells → competitive inhibition of <u>acetylcholine</u> (<u>ACh</u>) → <u>AChR</u> decay through <u>receptor</u> internalization (↓ <u>receptor</u> density at the postsynaptic membrane) and activation of <u>complement</u> (→ muscle cell lysis) → impaired <u>signal transduction</u> at the NMJ → <u>skeletal muscle</u> <u>weakness</u> and fatigue  

* Seropositive MG (80–90% of cases): positive assays for <u>antibodies</u> (in blood) against the <u>acetylcholine receptor</u> (<u>AChR-Ab</u>)

* Seronegative MG (10–20% of cases): negative for <u>AChR antibodies</u>, but may be positive for <u>muscle-specific tyrosine kinase antibodies</u> (<u>MuSK antibodies</u>)

## Clinical features

### Symptoms [[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)




Severity typically varies during the day and from day to day




* Fatigable <u>weakness</u> of <u>skeletal muscles</u> that worsens with increased muscle use and improves with rest.

* Generalized disease can involve all <u>skeletal muscles</u>, especially:

* <u>Eye muscles</u>: <u>diplopia</u>, blurred <u>vision</u> [[6]](/library/YsbntE)

* <u>Bulbar muscles</u>: <u>dysarthria</u>, difficulty chewing and/or <u>swallowing</u>, <u>dyspnea</u>

* <u>Proximal</u> muscles: difficulty standing from a chair, climbing stairs, brushing <u>hair</u> [[6]](/library/YsbntE)

* Respiratory muscles: <u>dyspnea</u>, <u>respiratory failure</u>

* Localized disease most commonly affects the <u>eye muscles</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Eye muscle</u> involvement is the most common initial symptom in generalized disease; larger muscles are involved later in the disease course. [[6]](/library/YsbntE)




### <u>Physical examination</u> findings [[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)




<u>Physical examination</u> may be completely normal in patients with myasthenia gravis, especially in mild cases.




* Normal <u>deep tendon reflexes</u>

* Limb <u>weakness</u> is typically symmetrical.

* Ocular <u>weakness</u> (e.g., <u>ptosis</u>) is typically asymmetrical. [[1]](/library/ZObZIF)

* Examination and proactive maneuvers can elicit typical ocular findings. [[1]](/library/ZObZIF)

* <u>Ice-pack test</u>: An ice pack placed on the affected <u>eyelid</u> for 5 minutes improves <u>ptosis</u> by â¥ 2 mm.  [[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)[[6]](/library/YsbntE)

* Curtain sign: Lifting the more ptotic <u>eyelid</u> worsens <u>ptosis</u> in the <u>contralateral</u> <u>eyelid</u>; eyebrow elevation and furrowing of the forehead can also occur.

* Cogan lid twitch sign: brief <u>eyelid</u> twitching when looking straight ahead after 10–20 seconds of downward gaze  [[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)

* Simpson test: historically used to reproduce <u>eyelid</u> fatigue; positive if looking upward for > 1 minute (without lifting the head) provokes <u>eyelid</u> fatigue





### Exacerbating factors of myasthenia gravis [[7]](/library/APaRhk)




The following factors may worsen symptoms of MG and/or trigger a <u>myasthenic crisis</u>.




* Infection

* <u>Surgery</u>, anesthesia

* <u>Pregnancy</u>, perimenstrual state [[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)

* Medications

* <u>Antibiotics</u> (e.g., <u>fluoroquinolones</u>, <u>aminoglycosides</u>, <u>macrolides</u>)

* Cardiovascular drugs (e.g., <u>procainamide</u>, <u>quinidine</u>, <u>beta blockers</u>)

* Psychiatric drugs (e.g., <u>chlorpromazine</u>, <u>risperidone</u>, <u>lithium</u>)

* <u>Glucocorticoids</u>

* <u>Magnesium</u>

* Contrast media

* <u>Stress</u>, temperature extremes

---

## Diagnosis

In patients with characteristic fatigable <u>muscle weakness</u>, confirm the diagnosis with serum <u>auto-antibodies</u> or; , if negative, by <u>electromyography</u> (<u>EMG</u>). [[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)[[6]](/library/YsbntE)




Results can confirm the diagnosis and be used to classify MG into subgroups depending on the <u>antibody</u> profile.




* Initial test: <u>anti-AChR antibodies</u> (highly specific for MG)  [[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)[[6]](/library/YsbntE)[[8]](/library/gfXFlx)

* Subsequent tests

* If initial <u>AChR-Ab</u> test is negative: anti-<u>MuSK antibodies</u>

* Further Ab testing in consultation with a <u>neurologist</u>   [[1]](/library/ZObZIF)[[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)





> [!TIP]
> Consider diagnostic studies for other autoimmune disorders (e.g., <u>Hashimoto thyroiditis</u>, <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>, <u>SLE</u>) in patients with suggestive symptoms.




### Additional studies [[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)[[6]](/library/YsbntE)




* <u>EMG</u> of affected muscles  [[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)

* Indication: patients with <u>clinical features of myasthenia gravis</u> and negative <u>autoantibodies</u>

* Findings: decremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation

* Chest CT: : indicated in all patients with confirmed myasthenia gravis to assess for a <u>thymoma</u> or <u>thymic</u> <u>hyperplasia</u>

* Edrophonium test: administration of a rapid-acting, short-duration <u>acetylcholinesterase inhibitor</u> to assess for symptom improvement in patients with suspected myasthenia gravis   

* Historically used to diagnose myasthenia gravis; currently replaced by the more specific and sensitive <u>anti-AChR antibody</u> test

* No longer available in the U.S.





> [!TIP]
> The <u>edrophonium test</u> was discontinued by the <u>FDA</u> in 2018 because of high <u>false-positive rates</u>.

## Differential diagnoses

### Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (<u>LEMS</u>) [[9]](/library/Ry1lUj0)




* Definition: rare <u>neuromuscular junction</u> disorder characterized by <u>proximal</u> <u>muscle weakness</u> and <u>autonomic dysfunction</u>

* Etiology

* Paraneoplastic: associated with small-cell <u>lung carcinoma</u> (in ⅔ of patients with <u>LEMS</u>)

* Primary autoimmune disorder

* Pathophysiology: <u>autoantibodies</u> directed against presynaptic <u>voltage-gated calcium channels</u> (anti-VGCC antibodies) → ↓ <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> influx → ↓ presynaptic <u>vesicle</u> fusion → impaired <u>acetylcholine</u> release in the NMJ

* Clinical features

* <u>Proximal</u> <u>muscle weakness</u>; muscle strength improves with repetitive or ongoing use

* Reduced or absent reflexes

* Autonomic symptoms

* Dry mouth

* <u>Constipation</u>

* Erectile and ejaculatory dysfunction

* Orthostatic dysregulation

* Diagnostics

* <u>Physical examination</u>

* Active muscle contraction or repeated muscle tapping increases reflex activity.

* Lambert sign: hand grip strength gradually increases over several seconds [[10]](/library/Dy11hj0)

* <u>EMG</u>: Repetitive nerve stimulation results in incremental responses.

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: <u>anti-VGCC antibodies</u> in serum

* Other: CT chest, abdomen, and <u>pelvis</u> to screen for underlying <u>malignancy</u>

* Treatment [[11]](/library/t2XXjx)

* Paraneoplastic <u>LEMS</u>: Treat the underlying <u>malignancy</u>.

* First-line to improve neuromuscular transmission: amifampridine

* <u>Orphan drug</u> used as first-line treatment of <u>Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome</u>

* Blockade of presynaptic <u>potassium</u> channels → ↑ AP duration → ↑ presynaptic <u>calcium</u> concentrations





#### Comparison of Myasthenia gravis and <u>LEMS</u>




| <br>Myasthenia gravis vs. <u>Lambert-Eaton</u> myasthenic syndrome <br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Myasthenia gravis | <u>Lambert-Eaton</u> myasthenic syndrome |
| Associated diseases | <br>* <u>Thymoma</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Small-cell lung cancer</u><br><br> |
| <u>Weakness</u> | <br><br>* Starts with <u>weakness</u> of the <u>extraocular muscles</u><br><br>* Worsens with exercise and throughout the day<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Starts with <u>weakness</u> of <u>proximal</u> limb muscles<br><br>* Improves with exercise and throughout the day<br><br><br> |
| Reflexes | <br>* Normal<br><br> | <br>* Reduced or absent<br><br> |
| Repetitive nerve stimulation | <br>* Decremental response<br><br> | <br>* Incremental response<br><br> |
| <u>Autonomic dysfunction</u> | <br>* None<br><br> | <br>* Common<br><br> |
| Response to <u>cholinesterase inhibitors</u> | <br>* Symptomatic relief<br><br> | <br>* No response<br><br> |





![Comparison between myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton syndromes](media/t1hpli6bw55ya1szg2vf0fi6.jpg)

### Other differential diagnoses




* Congenital myasthenic syndrome

* Genetic defects in <u>proteins</u> of the <u>neuromuscular junction</u> (NMJ) lead to neuromuscular disease.

* Presents similarly to myasthenia gravis (depending on the type of defect), but typically starts during <u>infancy</u> or childhood

* <u>Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis</u>

* <u>Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia</u> (for ocular symptoms)





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### General principles




* For patients with MG and difficulty breathing, admit to the hospital to rule out or treat <u>myasthenic crisis</u>.

* Provide supportive therapy and avoid exacerbating factors for myasthenia gravis.

* Treatment aims to control symptoms but is not curative.

* Titrate pharmacotherapy to minimize adverse effects, usually in consultation with a <u>neurologist</u>.

* Refer for thymectomy based on disease subtype and adequacy of pharmacological symptom management.





### Supportive therapy [[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)




* Provide <u>age-appropriate immunizations</u>; see “Overview of <u>ACIP</u> <u>Immunization</u> Schedule.”

* Encourage low-to-moderate intensity physical activity, and provide <u>obesity management</u>.

* Correct visual impairment.

* Educate patients about common <u>exacerbating factors of MG</u> (e.g., <u>fluoroquinolones</u>).





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid the use of <u>muscle relaxants</u>, <u>fluoroquinolones</u>, <u>macrolides</u>, and <u>aminoglycosides</u> in patients with myasthenia gravis because of the risk of worsening <u>muscle weakness</u>. [[12]](/library/_915JQ0)




### Pharmacotherapy




* <u>Cholinesterase inhibitor</u>: : first-line agent is <u>pyridostigmine</u> DOSAGE titrated to symptom relief   [[6]](/library/YsbntE)

* <u>Immunosuppressants</u> (<u>off-label</u>)

* Indications: inadequate symptom control with (or intolerance to) <u>pyridostigmine</u>

* Common initial regimen: <u>glucocorticoids</u> and/or <u>azathioprine</u>  [[1]](/library/ZObZIF)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Glucocorticoids</u> may be a part of the <u>management of myasthenia gravis</u>; however, caution is required as they have been associated with myasthenic crises in 9–18% of patients, especially within the first two weeks of initiating treatment. [[7]](/library/APaRhk)[[12]](/library/_915JQ0)




### Thymectomy [[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)




* Consider for:

* Most patients with <u>thymoma</u>, based on surgical <u>risk factors</u> and adequacy of medical management

* Select patients without <u>thymoma</u> in whom immunotherapy is not successful or not tolerated

* Potential benefits include:

* Reduced symptoms and exacerbations

* Decreased doses of pharmacotherapy





> [!TIP]
> Patients with rare subtypes of MG (e.g., <u>MuSK-Ab</u>) generally do not benefit from thymectomy. [[12]](/library/_915JQ0)

## Complications

### Myasthenic crisis [[6]](/library/YsbntE)[[7]](/library/APaRhk)




* Definition: acute, life-threatening exacerbation of myasthenic symptoms that leads to <u>respiratory failure</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Affects 15–20% of patients with myasthenia gravis  [[6]](/library/YsbntE)[[7]](/library/APaRhk)

* Most commonly occurs within 3 years of disease onset [[6]](/library/YsbntE)

* Precipitating factors: unidentifiable in up to 50% of cases [[7]](/library/APaRhk)

* Physiologic <u>stress</u>, e.g., infection (most common), <u>surgery</u>, anesthesia, <u>pregnancy</u>

* Medications

* See also “<u>Exacerbating factors of myasthenia gravis</u>.”

* Differential diagnosis: <u>cholinergic crisis</u> due to an excessive dose of <u>acetylcholinesterase inhibitors</u> (very rare) [[7]](/library/APaRhk)

* Management: Treat as a life-threatening emergency in consultation with <u>neurology</u> and critical care. [[5]](/library/Iv1YYQ0)

* Consider serial <u>spirometry</u> and <u>respiratory muscle function</u> testing.

* Intubate early if risk of <u>respiratory failure</u> is high, e.g.: [[13]](/library/D1W1Q40)

* Increasing generalized <u>weakness</u>, <u>dysphonia</u>, or <u>dyspnea</u> at rest

* <u>Vital capacity</u> < 15 mL/kg or <u>maximal inspiratory pressure</u> is less negative than –30 cm H<sub>2</sub>O

* Follow <u>ventilation strategy for neuromuscular weakness</u>.

* Review new medications; consider stopping known <u>exacerbating factors of myasthenia gravis</u>. [[12]](/library/_915JQ0)

* Consider pharmacotherapy with specialist guidance.

* High-dose <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE

* PLUS <u>IVIg</u>;  DOSAGE or plasma exchange [[7]](/library/APaRhk)





> [!TIP]
> ∼ 60–90% of patients with myasthenic crises require <u>intubation</u> with <u>mechanical ventilation</u>. Elective <u>intubation</u> is preferred over emergent <u>intubation</u>. [[7]](/library/APaRhk)




#### Differential diagnosis of <u>myasthenic crisis</u> and <u>cholinergic crisis</u>




| Myasthenic crisis vs. cholinergic crisis |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Myasthenic crisis</u> | <u>Cholinergic crisis</u> |
| Shared symptoms | <br><br>* <u>Muscle weakness</u><br><br>* <u>Dyspnea</u><br><br>* Sweating<br><br>* <u>Agitation</u><br><br>* <u>Disorientation</u><br><br>* Drowsiness<br><br>* Urinary and <u>fecal urgency</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Pupil</u> | <br>* Normal<br><br> | <br>* <u>Miosis</u><br><br> |
| <u>Fasciculations</u> | <br>* None<br><br> | <br>* Present<br><br> |
| <u>Heart rate</u> | <br>* <u>Tachycardia</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Bradycardia</u><br><br> |
| <u>Skin</u> | <br>* Cold and faint<br><br> | <br>* Warm and flushed<br><br> |
| Bronchial secretion | <br>* Normal<br><br> | <br>* Increased<br><br> |





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

## Special patient groups

### Myasthenia gravis during pregnancy [[14]](/library/ukcppc0)




* Risk of developing myasthenia gravis is increased in pregnant and postpartum individuals.

* Myasthenic symptoms often worsen during <u>pregnancy</u>, most commonly during the <u>first trimester</u>.

* Pregnant individuals are at increased risk of <u>myasthenic crisis</u>.

* <u>Cesarean sections</u> are commonly required for pregnant patients with MG because of ineffective contractions due to <u>muscle weakness</u> and risk of exhaustion during vaginal delivery.

* In about 10% of cases, <u>newborns</u> develop transient neonatal myasthenia (due to the transfer of maternal <u>antibodies</u>), which usually manifests with <u>swallowing</u> and sucking difficulties.





> [!WARNING]
> In the case of <u>preeclampsia</u>, individuals with myasthenia gravis should not be treated with <u>magnesium sulfate</u> since it worsens myasthenia symptoms.
